Here are your four palettes, each with a different design goal:

## Main — 8 Colors (Colorblind-Friendly)

Colorblind friendliness was the primary constraint here. The 8 colors were chosen to span hue, luminance, and saturation simultaneously — so they remain distinguishable even under deuteranopia/protanopia (red-green) or tritanopia (blue-yellow). The key strategy: no two adjacent colors rely solely on a red-vs-green distinction; the amber yellow and lime green are separated by teal.


| Hex | Distro | Role in palette |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| `#A80030` | Debian | Dark red anchor |
| `#E95420` | Ubuntu | Vivid orange |
| `#FAA41A` | Pop!_OS | Warm amber |
| `#87CF3E` | Linux Mint | Lime green |
| `#00D2CF` | CachyOS | Teal bridge |
| `#0B57A4` | Fedora | Mid blue |
| `#243365` | MX Linux | Dark navy |
| `#7B2FBE` | EndeavourOS | Purple |

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Additional — 8 Colors

These 8 fill the leftover hue bands with their own spread across the wheel. Notably, the dataset is blue-heavy, so this palette intentionally front-loads the green family (openSUSE, Manjaro, Void) before transitioning into the lighter/mid blues (Arch, elementary, NixOS, AlmaLinux).

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Larger — 12 Colors

The larger palette is the main 8 extended with 4 perceptual gap-fillers: Garuda's flame red sits between Debian's dark red and Ubuntu's orange; Manjaro's green fills the gap between lime and teal; Arch's cyan-blue bridges teal and Fedora's mid-blue; and NixOS's periwinkle bridges the navy-to-purple step. This gives a nearly even hue-wheel spread with no large jumps.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## Max — All 20, Paired Order

Inspired by ColorBrewer's *Paired* scheme, colors are arranged in 10 dark/light sibling pairs  — each consecutive two share a hue family. This makes it easy to encode two related categorical groups with a single palette (e.g., "base distros" vs. "derivatives"). The pairing order: `red → orange → yellow-green → green → forest/teal → cyan → light blue → steel blue → cobalt → navy/purple`.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## R Usage Snippet

Here's how to plug any of these directly into ggplot2:

```r
scale_main <- c(
  "#A80030", "#E95420", "#FAA41A", "#87CF3E",
  "#00D2CF", "#0B57A4", "#243365", "#7B2FBE"
)

scale_color_linux_main <- function(...) {
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = scale_main, ...)
}
scale_fill_linux_main <- function(...) {
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = scale_main, ...)
}

# Usage
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_linux_main()
```

> **⚠️ Watch Out**
> - `scale_color_manual()` will **silently recycle or drop** colors if your factor has more levels than values in the vector — always check `nlevels(your_factor) <= length(scale_main)`.
> - The paired scale only looks intentional if your data is **ordered consistently** — if ggplot reorders factor levels alphabetically, the pairing breaks. Use `factor(..., levels = your_order)` explicitly before plotting.
